This stability was attributed to sluggish demand from the feedlot market. In contrast, the malting barley market saw significantly different conditions. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In October 2025, the U.S. Grains & BioProducts Council (USGBC) and its members engaged with brewing industry leaders in Southeast Asia to promote U.S. malt and barley. The delegation held workshops and meetings in Vietnam with craft maltsters, beverage suppliers, and traders before traveling to Bangkok, Thailand. In Bangkok, the group participated in Brew Asia 2025, which took place from October 16-17 at the Bangkok International Trade & Exhibition Centre (BITEC). At the trade fair, the USGBC hosted an exhibition booth to showcase the quality of U.S. products to potential buyers from across Asia's growing beer market. The mission aimed to develop new market opportunities, particularly in Vietnam, the region's largest beer consumer, where there is significant interest in high-quality ingredients. <2> The 2025 North American barley crop is reported to be larger and of better quality than initially expected, overcoming early-season challenges. Despite drought conditions, high winds, and elevated temperatures from early May through mid-June, strong subsoil moisture sustained the crop. Favorable dry and warm weather in mid-August was ideal for ripening, leading to the positive outcome. Early sample results from western Canada indicate very good test weights, high levels of plump kernels, and lower protein levels than in 2024, with some areas in central Alberta reporting protein between 9-11%. Germination energy is noted as very high, and while there were some reports of pre-harvest sprouting, it does not appear widespread. Disease pressure from fusarium head blight was not a significant issue, with DON levels generally below 0.5 ppm. <3> The Idaho Barley Commission released its weekly grain market report on October 16, 2025, which provided cash prices for feed and malting barley as of the previous day, October 15, 2025. The report confirmed Idaho's position as the leading barley producer in the United States for 2025, accounting for 39% of the nation's total output. In 2025, the state produced 54.88 million bushels of barley from 490,000 harvested acres. This resulted in an average yield of 112 bushels per acre, tying a state record. <4> In mid-October 2025, barley markets showed minimal change, with buyers' bids generally remaining below $5.00/bu FOB farm. This price stability was attributed to strong yields across the prairies. An increased supply of other feed grains, such as corn and malt barley that did not meet grade specifications, also contributed to the market conditions. <5> On September 6, 2025, the Storm Prediction Center issued a forecast for scattered severe thunderstorms across the Northern Plains, a significant barley-producing area. The forecast indicated a 15% chance of damaging winds of 58 mph or greater and a 5% risk of large hail measuring 1 inch or larger, posing a potential threat to the region's standing barley crops. <6> A report analyzing price trends in 2025 noted that the global price of barley increased from $110.44 USD/ton in March 2025 to $117.83 USD/ton in June 2025. [1] This reflects a 6.7% increase over the three-month period. [1] The price had also seen an increase from $113.22 in April 2025. [5] <7> A report published on September 4, 2025, indicated that a projected record-large U.S. corn harvest is putting downward pressure on North American feed barley prices. The anticipated harvest is forecasted to be 425.26 million tonnes, which would surpass the previous record by 35.6 million tonnes. This massive influx of corn is specifically noted as pressuring Canadian feed barley prices. The U.S. corn harvest typically takes place in the fall, between August and October. <8> A USDA forecast, updated in its August 2025 Crop Production Report, revealed that U.S. barley planted area for 2025 is expected to be a record low of 2.28 million acres, a 4% decrease from the previous year. [1, 2] This projection revises an earlier estimate from the March 2025 Prospective Plantings report, which had anticipated a planted area of 2.32 million acres, a 2% decrease. [5, 6, 7, 8] The historically low production levels are contributing to concerns over tight supply chains for industries such as craft brewing. [2] The situation is exacerbated by expectations of another extremely hot year which, according to some analyses, will likely result in below-average yields for grains like barley. <9> In the U.S. Export Sales Report for the week ending July 31, 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported net sales reductions of 5,900 metric tons of barley for the 2025/2026 marketing year. [2] These reductions were attributed to sales for Canada (2,000 metric tons) being more than offset by reductions for Japan (8,000 metric tons). [2] Exports for the same period totaled 2,500 metric tons, with Canada receiving 2,200 metric tons and Japan receiving 300 metric tons. [2] This report, which provides a snapshot of international demand, covers transactions from July 25 through July 31, 2025. [2] <10> The U.S. Grains Council (USGC) hosted a delegation from a major international brewer based in Mexico for a tour of the U.S. barley value chain to build trade relationships for future purchases. The tour, which included stops in North Dakota and Idaho, was designed to showcase the sustainable growing practices of American barley farmers and to assure the brewer of grain quality during shipping. In North Dakota, the representatives attended educational sessions at the Northern Crops Institute and visited a local barley farm and a malting facility. The tour continued in Idaho with visits to the University of Idaho's Aberdeen Research and Extension Center to learn about barley breeding programs, and to member facility Mountain Malt to see its operations and nearby farms. The event is part of USGC's ongoing effort to connect international brewers with U.S. barley growers.
